# Breasts too fatty to measure


The rule of @sec-the-rule compares a patient only if both breasts have a usable scan. A breast with no usable scan is not
mismeasured; it is left out because every spot the beam hit was fat. Many of these breasts are genuinely NORMAL, and being too fatty to measure
is itself a result: that breast has little water. This section looks at those breasts, and at what happens if the test counts them as the
fattier breast instead of leaving the patient out.


## Who has no usable scan

Breasts with no usable scan, by label:

| Label | Breasts | No usable scan |
|---|---|---|
| NORMAL | 138 | 68 (49%) |
| BENIGN | 224 | 88 (39%) |
| CANCER | 76 | 33 (43%) |


And patients by how many of their breasts have a usable scan:

| Patients | All | Both breasts usable | One | Neither |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| CANCER vs NORMAL | 38 | 18 | 5 | 15 (39%) |
| BENIGN vs NORMAL | 52 | 27 | 6 | 19 (37%) |
| CANCER vs BENIGN | 24 | 5 | 9 | 10 (42%) |
| NORMAL vs NORMAL | 10 | 2 | 0 | 8 (80%) |


Of the 10 patients with two NORMAL breasts,
8 have no usable scan in either breast, so the rule never sees them (@fig-nn-fatty). These are the most typical healthy
patients in the study, and their breasts are fatty all the way through.

## Counting a fatty breast as a result

If a breast has no usable scan, the test can treat it as the fattier breast of the pair instead of dropping the patient. A patient whose
two breasts both have no usable scan is still left out: there is nothing to tell them apart.

| Comparison | Both breasts usable | Counting a breast with no usable scan as the fattier |
|---|---|---|
| CANCER vs NORMAL | 15/18 (83%), p = 0.008 | 18/23 (78%), p = 0.011 |
| BENIGN vs NORMAL | 10/27 (37%), p = 0.248 | 11/33 (33%), p = 0.080 |
| CANCER vs BENIGN | 2/5 (40%), p = 1.000 | 8/14 (57%), p = 0.791 |


For CANCER vs NORMAL this adds the patients where only the CANCER breast has a usable scan, which count as right, and those where only the
NORMAL breast has one, which count as wrong. The first kind outnumber the second, so more patients are compared with about the same strength
of evidence. For BENIGN vs NORMAL it goes the other way: more often it is the BENIGN breast that has no usable scan, and the result falls
further below chance. Most of the patients the rule drops are not lost wins, as in most of them both breasts are fatty.

Having two fatty breasts is much more common in NORMAL/NORMAL patients (80%)
than in any other kind of patient (37–42%). So "too fatty to measure in both breasts" leans towards a healthy patient. NORMAL/NORMAL patients
are older, though (median age 54
against 49 for the
other patients), and fatty breasts are common with age, so this may be age as much as health. With only
10 NORMAL/NORMAL patients it is a hint, not a result.
